To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the proportion of trees producing seeds increased over the 54 year study period for all tree species, but the standardized precipitation– evapotranspiration index (a measure of drought) contributed to the change in only two of the seven species.

temporal trends in seed production in seven dominant tree species in Europe over the past 50 years were primarily driven by increasing stand age, with drought contributing to temporal trends in two of the species, and that temporal variability and synchrony in seed production also increased in all species except Pinus sylvesris.

the increase in the proportion of seed-producing trees (PST), which is a measure of masting behavior, over time in European forest trees is mainly explained by stand age and that the temporal variability of PST increases with stand age in all species.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between climate and stand age in determining masting behavior of forest trees.
the relationship between climate change, stand age, masting, and seed production of temperate forest trees.
the relationship between climate change, stand age, masting, and the reproductive success of trees.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the climate change and the aging hypotheses are not mutually exclusive and that the aging of stands can explain a large part of the increase in masting in European temperate forests, but that climate change is also likely to be a factor.
the climate change and the aging hypotheses are not necessarily mutually exclusive and both may be important factors in driving temporal patterns of reproductive behavior in forest trees.
the temporal trend of PST is driven by the stand age, while climate is a secondary factor, but the effect of the climate is species specific.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aging is a major driver of masting behavior in European forest trees, while the role of climate change is more limited and species‐specific.
the temporal trends in mastication of trees is not only due to the climate change but also to the aging process of trees.
climate change and stand age are both important factors influencing the temporal dynamics of masting behavior in European forest trees.
The main takeaway from our work is that
plant ontogeny is an important confounding factor that should be considered when studying climate change effects on masting behavior in long‐term datasets.
aging is an important driver of temporal trends in mastication in forest trees, and this factor should be taken into account when analyzing long‐term data sets.
plant ontogeny can be an important driver of temporal changes in plant reproductive behavior, which should be taken into account when interpreting long‐term time trends in plant reproduction.
